summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in Mongolia's Criminal Code of 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is spread across several instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, prohibits discrimination on both grounds. Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. No comprehensive equality law is in place.

Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity directly. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 named gender identity and sexual orientation as protected grounds for hate crimes; it was scheduled for 1 September 2016 and took effect on 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed.

Legal gender recognition exists but is conditional. A June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows a person to change the legal gender recorded on their birth certificate or citizen identification card following sex reassignment surgery.

Constitutional marriage is restricted to a man and a woman. Article 16(11) of the Constitution defines marriage as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman who have reached the legally determined age, with State protection for family, motherhood and child. No partnership or union recognition is available to a trans visitor's relationship or to a couple read as same-sex under birth-sex status, and such households are ineligible for the protections afforded to opposite-sex couples.

Police practice shows documented, institution-level change alongside documented non-enforcement. After an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman in 2019, the LGBT Center trained police officers, prosecutors and judges on the 2017 hate-crime provisions; reporting in October 2019 puts the number trained at more than 500, and a figure of more than 300 was recorded in August 2018. The force has issued guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of the gender marker on identity documents. Against that, local reports and activists stated in August 2018 that police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBTQ people, with attacks often resulting in no punishment.

Trans-specific violence in the record is historical. In September 2009 three transgender women were kidnapped in broad daylight on a promenade in Ulaanbaatar by a hyper-nationalist group, driven to a cemetery on the city outskirts, beaten, sexually assaulted and forced to perform sexual acts on the perpetrators as a warning; the incident was not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. The dossier records no later trans-specific attack of this kind. Anti-LGBT violence more broadly is documented in 2001, when a lesbian woman was raped, abducted and stabbed by two men, and in February 2014, when a gay man was sexually assaulted by a neo-Nazi group; such violence is often not reported to police.
